displayQuote: If we have our own why in life, we shall get along with almost any how

meta.title: Who really said "If we have our own why in life, we shall get along with almost any how"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Yes, it's Nietzsche — from Twilight of the Idols (1889). The English wording is Walter Kaufmann's translation, popularized by Viktor Frankl, who credited Nietzsche.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'If we have our own why in life, we shall get along with almost any how'?
meta.ogDescription: Genuinely Nietzsche — Twilight of the Idols (1889), 'Maxims and Arrows,' 12. The English phrasing is Walter Kaufmann's translation.

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: From Twilight of the Idols (Götzen-Dämmerung, 1889), “Maxims and Arrows,” aphorism 12: “Hat man sein warum? des Lebens, so verträgt man sich fast mit jedem wie?” The familiar English wording is Walter Kaufmann’s translation in The Portable Nietzsche — which actually reads “why of life”; the widely shared form swaps in “why in life.”

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: English wording follows Walter Kaufmann, The Portable Nietzsche (1954)

source.excerpt: Hat man sein warum? des Lebens, so verträgt man sich fast mit jedem wie? — Der Mensch strebt nicht nach Glück; nur der Engländer thut das.
trail: Quote Investigator traces the saying to Nietzsche’s 1889 Twilight of the Idols and lays out the competing English renderings in its 2019 investigation ↗.
Wikiquote lists the line under Twilight of the Idols, “Maxims and Arrows,” giving the German original alongside the “why in life … almost any how ↗” wording.
Viktor Frankl popularized the aphorism in Man’s Search for Meaning (1946), but he explicitly credited Nietzsche ↗.
source.excerptNote: The German original, from “Sprüche und Pfeile” (Maxims and Arrows), 12. Kaufmann renders the first sentence “If we have our own why of life, we shall get along with almost any how.”
source.rightsHolder: Walter Kaufmann translation — Viking Press / Penguin Random House
source.rightsNote: Nietzsche’s German original (1889) is long in the public domain. But the exact English wording shown here traces to Walter Kaufmann’s translation in The Portable Nietzsche (first published 1954), which remains in copyright. The public-domain Victorian translations (Thomas Common, 1896; Anthony Ludovici, 1911) use markedly different phrasing, so the modern “why … almost any how” form is not itself public domain.

author.name: Friedrich Nietzsche
author.heading: About Friedrich Nietzsche
author.bio: Friedrich Nietzsche was a German philosopher whose work on morality, nihilism, and the will to power reshaped modern thought. Twilight of the Idols, written in 1888 and published in 1889, was one of his last works before his mental collapse; its opening “Maxims and Arrows” is a string of aphorisms, including the one about the ‘why’ and the ‘how’ of life.

misattribution.heading: The mix-ups
misattribution.intro: This one is correctly credited to Nietzsche — the usual confusion is over who made it famous and exactly how it’s worded.

items.why: Frankl quoted the line twice in Man’s Search for Meaning (1946) and it became inseparable from his work, so many now cite it as “Frankl’s.” But Frankl named Nietzsche as the source ↗ both times.
The most-shared form says “our own why in life,” but Kaufmann’s published translation reads “our own why of life.” Both render the same German line from Maxims and Arrows, 12 ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: The thought and the source are genuinely Nietzsche’s — Twilight of the Idols, 1889 — and the polished English wording is Walter Kaufmann’s translation ↗.

context.heading: Why it resonates
lead: Nietzsche buried the line in a rapid-fire list of maxims, but it carries one of his most portable ideas: that meaning (“why”) makes suffering and circumstance (“how”) bearable. Half a century later, Viktor Frankl — a psychiatrist who survived the Nazi camps — made it the emotional spine of Man’s Search for Meaning, which is why the two names are now so often linked.
context.pull: He who has a why can bear almost any how.
